title: Before the Bag Leaves: Platelet Swirl, Granulocyte ABO, Immediate Spin and the DIN
summary: Learn the last checks before a unit leaves the blood bank: why a platelet unit without swirling is held, when an immediate-spin crossmatch is enough, why granulocytes must be ABO compatible and given within 24 hours, and what the ISBT 128 donation identification number does.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 41 High-Yield Hits 12 (granulocytes ABO-compatible, room temperature, within 24 h), 15 (ISBT 128 DIN) and 21 (absent swirling) and Exam Trap 4 (immediate-spin crossmatch with a positive screen). Checked against the AABB Circular of Information (June 2024), the UK Red Book (JPAC, sections 7.4.1 and 7.6.1, read on the JPAC website), Singh 2009, García-Otálora 2025 (ISBT congress report), Tiwari 2017, Anu 2022, R A 2024, Adkins 2024, Agrawal 2022 and Distler 2010. Qualifications taught: a unit that swirls can still be bacterially contaminated (register flag rv-swirl-not-sterility); granulocytes are stored WITHOUT agitation and must be irradiated, and red-cell-reduced ABO-incompatible granulocytes are reported as an exception (rv-granulocyte-no-agitation). Not taught as fact: the trap’s electronic-crossmatch requirements (“no unexpected antibodies plus two ABO determinations”), which no source read in this session states; and Hit 13 (per-unit infection risks).

objectives: Explain what platelet swirling shows and what to do when it is absent.
State when an immediate-spin crossmatch is acceptable and what is needed when a clinically significant antibody is present.
Apply the ABO, storage, timing and irradiation rules for granulocyte transfusion.
Describe the structure and purpose of the ISBT 128 donation identification number.

scenes.title: Four bags at the issue window
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four requests reach the blood bank issue window at once. (1) A day-4 platelet pool that looks uniformly turbid with no shimmer when gently pressed against the light; (2) a granulocyte unit from a group A donor ordered for a group O recipient; (3) red cells for a patient whose antibody screen is positive and anti-E has been identified, with a request to “just do an immediate spin”; (4) a unit whose label carries a 13-character ISBT 128 donation identification number. Question token: “Which can leave the bank?”

cues.text: Four requests reach the issue window at once. A day-four platelet pool looks evenly cloudy, with no shimmer when it is held to the light.
A group A granulocyte unit is ordered for a group O patient, and a patient with anti-E needs red cells, with a request to just do an immediate spin.
The fourth unit carries an ISBT 128 donation number. Which of these can leave the bank?

scenes.title: What each check actually sees
scenes.altText: Schematic: four check cards. Swirl card: swirling is a visual pre-issue check; it reflects discoid (disc-shaped) platelets, and its absence indicates spherical, shape-changed platelets (Singh 2009; UK Red Book 7.4.1). Crossmatch card: the immediate-spin (IS) saline phase is done at room temperature to rule out IgM reactions; the antihuman globulin (AHG) phase detects non-agglutinating IgG antibodies. Granulocyte card: apheresis granulocytes contain 20–50 mL of red cells (AABB Circular). DIN card: the ISBT 128 donation identification number has three parts: a 5-character facility identification number assigned by ICCBBA, a 2-character year, and a 6-character serial number from the facility; it is globally unique for 100 years (Distler 2010).

cues.text: Swirling is the shimmer you see when a platelet bag is gently moved against the light. It comes from disc-shaped platelets. Spherical, shape-changed platelets do not swirl.
An immediate-spin crossmatch is a room-temperature saline test aimed at IgM reactions. The antiglobulin phase is what detects IgG antibodies that coat cells without clumping them.
A granulocyte unit is not just white cells: an apheresis granulocyte unit carries twenty to fifty millilitres of red cells.
And the ISBT 128 donation number has three parts: a five-character facility code assigned by ICCBBA, a two-digit year, and a six-character serial number, unique worldwide for one hundred years.

scenes.title: When each check says stop
scenes.altText: Rule cards. Swirl: blood components must be inspected immediately before use, and a unit with abnormal appearance must not be used and is followed up with the transfusion service (AABB Circular); in a 2024 ISBT congress report, a twin platelet pool that showed no swirling by day 4 was found to be bacterially contaminated, and pathogen-reduced units that failed the swirling test were quarantined as near misses. Crossmatch: immediate-spin crossmatch is used only when the antibody screen is negative and there is no history of red cell antibodies; with a positive screen, the antibody is identified and antigen-negative, AHG-crossmatch-compatible units are given (Tiwari 2017; Anu 2022). Granulocytes: the red cells must be ABO compatible with the recipient’s plasma; serologic compatibility must be established; store at 20–24 °C WITHOUT agitation for no more than 24 hours, and transfuse as soon as possible and within 24 hours of collection; irradiate; do not use leukocyte reduction filters (AABB Circular; Adkins 2024). UK Red Book: store at 22 ± 2 °C without agitation, start by midnight on the day after donation.

cues.text: Every unit is inspected just before issue, and a unit that looks abnormal is not used. In one 2024 report, a platelet pool that had stopped swirling by day four turned out to be contaminated with bacteria, and units that failed the swirl check were quarantined.

Immediate spin is acceptable only when the antibody screen is negative and there is no history of red cell antibodies. With anti-E, the lab gives E-negative units that are compatible in the antiglobulin crossmatch.

Because granulocytes carry red cells, those red cells must be ABO compatible with the patient’s plasma, and a crossmatch is needed. A group A unit cannot go to a group O patient, whose plasma has anti-A.

Granulocytes are given as soon as possible, within twenty-four hours of collection. If they must wait, they are kept at twenty to twenty-four degrees without agitation. They are irradiated and never given through a leukocyte filter.

props.title: No swirl → do not issue
lines: Contaminated twin pool lost its swirl

scenes.title: Back at the window
scenes.altText: Decision table for the hook. (1) Platelet pool with no swirl: do not issue; quarantine and investigate (possible shape change or bacterial contamination). (2) Group A granulocytes for a group O patient: not acceptable as issued — the red cells must be ABO compatible with the recipient’s plasma; choose a compatible donor (red-cell-reduced ABO-incompatible units are a specialist exception reported in case literature, not routine). (3) Anti-E: no immediate spin; give E-negative red cells compatible by AHG crossmatch. (4) DIN: the unit can be traced; the DIN supports traceability and rapid recall alerts, but it is an identifier, not a safety check. Caution card: a unit that swirls can still be contaminated — in the same report a pool from the same buffy-coat batch still swirled and caused a septic reaction.

cues.text: Back to the window. The platelet pool with no swirl stays: quarantine it and tell the transfusion service so it can be investigated.
The group A granulocytes cannot go to the group O patient. Pick a donor whose red cells are compatible with the patient’s plasma, and crossmatch.
The anti-E patient gets E-negative red cells crossmatched through the antiglobulin phase, not an immediate spin.

The DIN lets the unit be traced from donor to patient and recalled fast if a problem appears. But a number is not a safety check, and a swirl is not a sterility test: in that same report, the pool that still swirled caused a septic reaction.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Immediate spin is fine even with a positive antibody screen” (✓ IS only with a negative screen and no antibody history; otherwise antigen-negative units with an AHG crossmatch); “Granulocytes are white cells, so ABO does not matter” (✓ they carry 20–50 mL of red cells, which must be ABO compatible with the recipient’s plasma); “A platelet unit that swirls is safe” (✓ absent swirl means do not issue, but a swirling unit can still be contaminated).

cues.text: Trap one: immediate spin is fine even when the screen is positive. No: with an antibody, the lab needs antigen-negative units and an antiglobulin crossmatch.
Trap two: granulocytes are white cells, so ABO does not matter. No: each unit carries red cells that must be ABO compatible with the patient’s plasma.
Trap three: if a platelet bag swirls, it is safe. No: no swirl means do not issue, but swirling does not prove the unit is free of bacteria.

scenes.title: Shimmer, Screen, Same group, Stamp
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Four S’s at the issue window: SHIMMER (platelets must swirl), SCREEN (immediate spin only after a negative screen and clean history), SAME GROUP (granulocyte red cells ABO compatible with the patient’s plasma), STAMP (the DIN traces every bag).” Tokens: Shimmer · Screen · Same group · Stamp. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: four S’s at the issue window. Shimmer: platelets must swirl. Screen: immediate spin only after a negative screen. Same group: granulocyte red cells match the patient’s plasma. Stamp: the donation number traces every bag.

Where it breaks: a shimmer does not prove the unit is sterile; immediate spin also needs a clean antibody history; specialist centres sometimes remove red cells to give ABO-incompatible granulocytes; and the stamp identifies a unit without vouching for its safety.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “No swirl → quarantine (but swirl ≠ sterile) · immediate spin only with a negative screen and no antibody history”, “Granulocytes: ABO-compatible red cells, within 24 h, no agitation, irradiated · DIN = globally unique traceability”.

cues.text: Hold any platelet unit that does not swirl, use immediate spin only after a negative antibody screen with no antibody history, give granulocytes whose red cells are ABO compatible within twenty-four hours, and rely on the ISBT 128 donation number to trace every unit.

props.label: No swirl → hold (swirl ≠ sterile) · IS only if screen negative
Granulocytes: ABO-compatible red cells, ≤ 24 h · DIN = trace

explanation.what: Plain language: just before a unit leaves the blood bank, staff look at it, confirm the right compatibility test was done, and rely on a unique number to track it. Platelets should shimmer; a patient with an antibody needs a fuller crossmatch; granulocyte bags contain red cells, so ABO matters; and every bag has a worldwide-unique number. Scientific terms: swirling phenomenon, discoid vs spherical platelet morphology, immediate-spin (IS) crossmatch, antihuman globulin (AHG) crossmatch, type and screen, antigen-negative units, apheresis granulocytes, ISBT 128, donation identification number (DIN), facility identification number (FIN), traceability, recall.
explanation.why: Swirling reflects disc-shaped, functional platelets; loss of swirling signals shape change and has accompanied bacterial contamination. IS is a room-temperature phase aimed at IgM reactions, while IgG alloantibodies such as anti-E need the antiglobulin phase. Granulocyte units carry 20–50 mL of red cells, enough to cause hemolysis if ABO incompatible, and granulocyte function deteriorates quickly in storage. A globally unique DIN removes renumbering and supports donor-to-recipient tracing and rapid recall alerts.
explanation.measure: Inspect every unit immediately before use; abnormal appearance → do not use, follow up with the transfusion service. IS only with a negative antibody screen and no history of red cell antibodies; with an antibody, identify it and give antigen-negative, AHG-compatible units. Granulocytes: red cells ABO compatible with recipient plasma, serologic compatibility established, transfuse as soon as possible and within 24 h of collection, store at 20–24 °C without agitation if needed, irradiate, no leukocyte reduction filter (UK: 22 ± 2 °C, start by midnight on the day after donation). DIN: 5-character FIN + 2-character year + 6-character serial, unique for 100 years.
explanation.differs: IS crossmatch (room temperature, IgM) vs AHG crossmatch (IgG); swirl present (discoid) vs absent (spherical, hold); granulocytes (red cells present, ABO matters, no agitation, no leukocyte filter) vs platelets (agitated storage); DIN (identifier) vs safety testing.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the action for a non-swirling platelet unit, the crossmatch for a patient with an identified alloantibody, the correct statement about granulocyte compatibility and timing, or the purpose of the DIN.

questions.stem: During pre-issue inspection, a day-4 platelet pool shows no swirling when gently moved against the light. The bag is intact and the colour looks normal. What is the best action?

options.text: Do not issue it; quarantine it and report it for investigation
options.rationale: Correct. Absent swirling signals shape-changed platelets and has accompanied bacterial contamination; a unit with abnormal appearance must not be used.

options.text: Issue it, because the bag is intact and the colour is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Swirling is a separate pre-issue check; an intact, normally coloured bag can still lack it.

options.text: Warm it to 37 °C to restore swirling, then issue it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Platelets are kept at 20–24 °C; warming does not make a doubtful unit safe and delays the investigation.

options.text: Issue it only to a patient who is not bleeding
options.rationale: Incorrect. A possibly contaminated or nonviable unit should not go to any patient.

questions.stem: A patient’s antibody screen is positive and anti-E is identified. Red cells are requested for transfusion. Which compatibility approach is appropriate?

options.text: E-negative red cells that are compatible in an antiglobulin (AHG) crossmatch
options.rationale: Correct. With an identified clinically significant antibody, antigen-negative units are crossmatched through the antiglobulin phase.

options.text: Any ABO-compatible unit after an immediate-spin crossmatch
options.rationale: Incorrect. Immediate spin is used only when the screen is negative and there is no antibody history; it is a room-temperature phase that is not designed to detect IgG antibodies like anti-E.

options.text: Any ABO-compatible unit with no crossmatch, because only one antibody is present
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single clinically significant antibody still requires antigen-negative, crossmatch-compatible units.

options.text: Repeat the antibody screen until it becomes negative, then use immediate spin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Once a clinically significant antibody has been identified, the patient no longer meets the negative-screen, clean-history condition for immediate spin; antigen-negative, AHG-compatible units are given.

questions.stem: An apheresis granulocyte unit is ordered for a neutropenic patient with a fungal infection. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its red cells must be ABO compatible with the patient’s plasma, and it should be transfused within 24 hours of collection
options.rationale: Correct. The unit contains 20–50 mL of red cells, and granulocyte function deteriorates in storage, so it is given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.

options.text: ABO compatibility is unnecessary because granulocytes are white cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. The red cells in the unit can cause hemolysis if ABO incompatible.

options.text: It should be stored at 20–24 °C with continuous agitation, like platelets
options.rationale: Incorrect. Granulocytes are stored without agitation if storage is unavoidable.

options.text: It should be given through a leukocyte reduction filter to lower febrile reactions
options.rationale: Incorrect. Leukocyte reduction filters remove the granulocytes that are the point of the transfusion.

claims.text: Swirling reflects discoid platelets, absence indicates spherical forms; visual swirl check before issue; abnormal units not used and followed up.
Absent swirling has accompanied bacterial contamination, yet a contaminated unit can still swirl.

Immediate-spin crossmatch only with a negative antibody screen and no antibody history; antibody present → antigen-negative AHG-compatible units; IS is a room-temperature phase for IgM, AHG detects IgG.
Granulocytes contain 20–50 mL red cells; ABO compatible with recipient plasma; crossmatch; within 24 h; 20–24 °C without agitation; irradiate; no leukocyte reduction filter.
Red-cell-reduced ABO-incompatible granulocyte transfusion is reported as an exception.
DIN structure (5 + 2 + 6 characters), global uniqueness for 100 years, traceability and recall support.
Reviewer: electronic crossmatch requires no unexpected antibodies plus two ABO determinations. Not taught; no source read in this session states the criteria.
Scenario invented; bags and labels schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says absent swirling means suspect nonviable platelets or bacterial contamination. García-Otálora 2025 confirms a non-swirling twin pool was contaminated, but the transfused pool from the same batch still swirled and caused a septic reaction, so the presence of swirling does not exclude contamination. The lesson teaches both halves.

The reviewer says granulocytes are “stored at room temperature”. The AABB Circular and UK Red Book specify storage WITHOUT agitation (unlike platelets), mandatory irradiation and no leukocyte reduction filter; a case report describes red-cell-reduced ABO-incompatible units. The UK Red Book times transfusion to start by midnight on the day after donation rather than a strict 24 hours.
The trap’s electronic-crossmatch criteria (no unexpected antibodies plus two ABO determinations) could not be checked against an open source in this session; not taught.
Storage, timing and compatibility rules come from the US AABB Circular and the UK Red Book; Philippine regulations and local blood bank SOPs are not covered.
